name: Client lifetime value playbook
summary:
**Conversation Overview**

The person requested help creating a client-facing KPI reference playbook for med spa owners, specifically for The Luxora Collective (theluxoracollective.co). The goal was a clean, no-fluff document that clients could receive immediately upon onboarding to help them understand and track their core business metrics. A key requirement was including a step-by-step Lifetime Value (LTV) per client calculation alongside the broader KPI set.

Claude produced a formatted DOCX playbook covering ten KPIs: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC), Average Order Value (AOV), Client Lifetime Value (LTV), LTV to CAC Ratio, Gross Margin Per Treatment, Contribution Margin, Break-Even Treatments Per Month, Revenue Per Patient (RPP), Provider Utilization Rate, and Marketing Payback Period. Each KPI block included a formula, plain-English explanation, and a fill-in "Your Numbers" column. LTV was given a featured section at the top with an input table, worked example, and a side-by-side completion box. The document used The Luxora Collective's brand colors (dark navy and gold) and closed with a section showing how all metrics connect in sequence.

The person's stated preference was for simplicity and directness with no extra content, which shaped the tight, structured format used throughout. Claude also flagged two areas for potential improvement after delivery: the "Avg. Years as Client" default of two years could produce inflated LTV figures without real retention data validation, and the Contribution Margin block was identified as the most conceptually abstract section, with a suggestion to add a worked failure example to make the lesson more concrete for non-finance-background owners.

10 Core Financial Formulas
Every Med Spa Owner Must Know
Operate profitably, scale safely, and make data-driven decisions around marketing, staffing, and growth.

1.  Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
FORMULA
CAC = Total Marketing + Sales Spend  /  New Customers Acquired

WHY IT MATTERS
CAC reveals the true cost of bringing one new patient through your door. For a med spa, this includes digital ads, social media spend, influencer partnerships, referral incentives, and any staff time devoted to sales or outreach.
If your CAC is $150 but a new patient only spends $180 on their first visit, you are essentially breaking even before factoring in overhead. However, if that same patient returns several times per year over multiple years, a $150 CAC may be very well spent.
Tracking CAC by channel (Google Ads vs. Instagram vs. referrals) lets you invest more in what works and cut what does not. Many med spas discover that word-of-mouth referrals have a near-zero CAC and the highest loyalty rates, which makes referral programs a high-priority strategy.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Benchmark: A healthy CAC for med spas typically runs $75 to $250, depending on your market and services.
Track CAC separately by channel so you know which marketing is actually working.
If CAC is climbing, audit your ad targeting, landing pages, and follow-up processes before spending more.

2.  Average Order Value (AOV)
FORMULA
AOV = Total Revenue  /  Number of Transactions

WHY IT MATTERS
AOV tells you how much the average patient spends per visit. A higher AOV means you are generating more revenue from the patients you already have, which is almost always more cost-effective than acquiring new ones.
In a med spa context, AOV is directly influenced by how well your team recommends complementary services. A patient coming in for Botox may also be an ideal candidate for a skin consultation or a retail skincare product. Without a structured upsell and add-on process, that revenue is left on the table every single visit.
Memberships and packages are powerful AOV levers. When a patient pre-pays for a bundle of services, their per-visit AOV rises and you benefit from improved cash flow and retention at the same time.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Train providers and front desk staff to naturally recommend complementary services at every appointment.
Bundle popular treatments into packages priced at a slight discount to encourage higher upfront spend.
Retail product sales are a high-margin AOV booster. Display and recommend strategically.

3.  Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
FORMULA
LTV = Average Visit Value  x  Visits Per Year  x  Average Retention (Years)

WHY IT MATTERS
LTV is arguably the single most important number in your entire business. It answers the question: how much is one patient truly worth to your practice over the course of your relationship with them?
A patient who spends $300 per visit, comes in four times per year, and stays with you for five years has an LTV of $6,000. That context completely changes how you think about spending $200 to acquire them. Without knowing your LTV, you are making marketing and pricing decisions in the dark.
LTV also has a retention dimension that is often overlooked. Improving your average retention from 2 years to 3 years on the same patient does not just add one year of revenue. It can increase LTV by 50% with zero additional marketing spend. This is why patient experience, follow-up communication, and loyalty programs are not just nice-to-haves. They are financial strategy.
Med spas that focus on retention alongside acquisition consistently out-earn those that treat every month like a new customer race.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Survey lapsed patients to understand why they stopped coming. Even a small improvement in retention drives large LTV gains.
Build a membership program to formalize and extend retention.
Segment your LTV by service type. Neurotoxin patients often have high natural repeat rates. Body contouring patients may be lower frequency but higher value per visit.

4.  LTV to CAC Ratio
FORMULA
LTV:CAC Ratio = LTV  /  CAC

WHY IT MATTERS
The LTV:CAC ratio is your growth engine health score. It tells you whether your investment in acquiring new patients is sustainable and appropriately scaled.
A ratio below 2x means you are spending nearly as much to get a patient as they will ever return to you. This is a warning sign that you may be overspending on acquisition, underperforming on retention, or underpricing your services.
A ratio between 3x and 5x is considered healthy for most service businesses including med spas. You are acquiring patients efficiently, retaining them well, and generating meaningful returns on your marketing investment.
A ratio above 6x is a strong signal that you are actually underinvesting in growth. You have a highly efficient model and more marketing spend could produce significant returns. Many owners with a 6x+ ratio are leaving substantial revenue on the table by being too conservative with their ad budgets.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Calculate this ratio quarterly and track the trend over time.
If below 3x, focus on retention improvements before increasing ad spend.
If consistently above 6x, consider scaling your marketing budget. Your economics support it.

5.  Gross Margin Per Treatment
FORMULA
Gross Margin = (Revenue - Direct Costs)  /  Revenue

Direct costs include: injectables, provider labor, consumables, and disposables
WHY IT MATTERS
Gross margin per treatment tells you how much of each service dollar actually stays in the business after paying for the direct cost of delivering that service. It is the foundation of profitability analysis at the treatment level.
Not all treatments are created equal. A treatment generating $400 in revenue with $300 in direct costs has a 25% gross margin. One generating $300 with $60 in direct costs has an 80% margin. Volume of the first treatment can never compensate for its thin margin if your overhead is significant.
This formula should be calculated for every service you offer, not just your highest-revenue ones. Med spas frequently discover that their most promoted or most popular treatments are among their least profitable. Marketing a low-margin service harder does not fix the margin problem. It just increases revenue and workload without proportional profit.
Identifying your highest-margin treatments allows you to build your marketing strategy, provider incentives, and upsell sequences around them intentionally.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Run this calculation for every service in your menu at least once per year.
Consider adjusting pricing on low-margin services or reducing them in favor of higher-margin alternatives.
Negotiate injectable pricing with suppliers regularly. Even a 10% reduction in product cost can shift margins meaningfully.

6.  Contribution Margin
FORMULA
Contribution Margin = Revenue - Variable Costs - CAC

WHY IT MATTERS
While gross margin shows profitability at the treatment level before marketing costs, contribution margin includes your cost to acquire that patient. This makes it a more complete picture of true per-patient profitability.
A treatment may have a 70% gross margin, but if it required $200 in marketing spend to attract that patient for a $250 service, the contribution margin tells a very different story. After variable costs and CAC, you may have almost nothing left to contribute toward covering your fixed overhead.
Contribution margin is especially useful when evaluating new service launches, promotions, or Groupon-style deals. These tactics often attract high volumes of patients at artificially low margins with no guarantee of retention. Calculating the true contribution margin reveals whether these campaigns are actually building a profitable patient base or just creating activity without financial progress.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Use contribution margin to evaluate whether discount promotions are worth running.
If a campaign drives volume but contribution margin is near zero, the business gains no financial benefit despite the busy schedule.
Track contribution margin trends over time to measure the improving or declining profitability of your growth activities.

7.  Break-Even Number of Treatments
FORMULA
Break-Even Treatments = Fixed Monthly Costs  /  Contribution Margin Per Treatment

WHY IT MATTERS
Every med spa has a monthly floor it must exceed before it earns a single dollar of profit. Rent, base salaries, insurance, software subscriptions, and other fixed costs accumulate whether you see one patient or one hundred. The break-even formula tells you exactly how many treatments you need to perform each month just to keep the lights on.
This number is essential for operational planning. If your break-even is 85 treatments per month and you are currently performing 70, you are operating at a loss regardless of how busy the schedule feels. Knowing this number turns a vague sense of financial stress into a specific, actionable target.
Break-even analysis also helps you evaluate business decisions proactively. Before signing a new lease, hiring a provider, or adding expensive equipment, you can calculate how many additional treatments per month would be required to cover the new fixed cost. If that number is not realistic given your current capacity and patient volume, the decision warrants more caution.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Post your break-even treatment count somewhere visible so your team understands the baseline goal every month.
Recalculate any time you add a significant fixed cost such as a new provider, new equipment, or expanded space.
Use this number in your monthly financial review as the first benchmark before evaluating profit.

8.  Revenue Per Patient (RPP)
FORMULA
RPP = Total Revenue  /  Total Unique Patients

WHY IT MATTERS
Revenue per patient measures the depth of your relationships, not just the number of them. Two practices can have the same total patient count but vastly different RPP figures, reflecting entirely different business models and growth trajectories.
A low RPP suggests your patient base is transactional. People come in once or twice, often for entry-level services, and do not return. A high RPP indicates that patients are returning regularly, purchasing multiple service types, and potentially enrolled in memberships. The latter business is far more stable and scalable.
RPP also serves as an indirect measure of patient education and trust. Patients who understand the full range of services you offer, who trust their provider, and who see ongoing results tend to invest more deeply in their care. This means that investing in patient communication, treatment planning conversations, and provider-patient relationship quality has a direct and measurable impact on RPP over time.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Segment RPP by patient cohort and acquisition year to understand whether newer patients are generating as much revenue as older ones.
If RPP is low, review your consultation and treatment planning process. Are providers presenting comprehensive care options?
Membership programs almost always increase RPP by encouraging regular visits and multi-service engagement.

9.  Utilization Rate
FORMULA
Utilization Rate = Booked Treatment Hours  /  Available Treatment Hours

WHY IT MATTERS
Utilization rate measures how efficiently you are converting your most finite resource, provider time, into revenue. A provider working a full eight-hour shift but only performing five hours of billable treatments has a utilization rate of 62.5%. The remaining time is generating zero revenue while still incurring full labor cost.
Low utilization is one of the most insidious profit drains in a med spa because it is invisible on a busy-feeling schedule. Gaps between appointments, no-shows without same-day replacements, admin tasks during prime hours, and long treatment setup times all reduce utilization without anyone necessarily noticing.
Improving utilization from 65% to 80% on the same provider can add tens of thousands of dollars in annual revenue with no additional overhead. This is why online booking optimization, no-show reduction strategies (deposits, reminders, confirmation sequences), and schedule management practices are so financially significant. They are utilization tools, not just convenience features.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Target a utilization rate of 75% to 85% for providers. Below 70% is a sign of inefficiency. Above 90% consistently may indicate understaffing.
Require deposits on appointments to reduce no-shows, which are the single biggest utilization killer.
Analyze utilization by time of day and day of week to identify patterns and develop targeted promotions for slow periods.

10.  Marketing Payback Period
FORMULA
Payback Period = CAC  /  Monthly Gross Profit Per Patient

WHY IT MATTERS
The marketing payback period tells you how many months it takes to recover what you spent to acquire a patient. This is a cash flow metric as much as a profitability metric, and it is especially important for growing practices that are actively investing in marketing.
If your CAC is $180 and a patient generates $60 in monthly gross profit (via a membership or regular visit cadence), your payback period is three months. That is a very healthy return. If your CAC is $180 but patients only visit twice a year generating $40 in gross profit per visit, your payback period stretches to over two years, during which time that patient could leave and the investment is only partially recovered.
Payback period is also a useful tool for evaluating different marketing channels against each other. A channel that produces patients with a six-month payback period is not necessarily worse than one with a two-month payback if the longer-payback patients have dramatically higher LTV. Used alongside LTV:CAC, payback period gives you a full picture of your marketing investment quality.
ACTIONABLE TIPS
Membership programs shorten payback periods significantly by guaranteeing regular monthly revenue from acquired patients.
If payback exceeds 12 months, reconsider the marketing channel or patient segment generating those results.
Track payback period by acquisition source to identify which channels produce faster-returning investments.

The Big Picture
Sustainable med spa growth is not built on any single metric. It is built on understanding how these formulas connect to each other and amplify each other.
Marketing Spend drives your CAC. CAC relative to LTV determines whether growth is sustainable. Gross Margin per Treatment determines how much of each dollar of LTV actually survives to become profit. Utilization Rate determines how efficiently your capacity translates into revenue. And Break-Even analysis grounds all of it in the reality of your fixed cost structure.
Owners who track these numbers monthly do not make decisions based on how busy they feel or how full the schedule looks. They make decisions based on what the data actually says. That is the difference between surviving and scaling.
Marketing Spend  -->  CAC  -->  LTV  -->  Margin  -->  Cash Flow

1	---
     2	name: docx
     3	description: "Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation."
     4	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     5	---
     6	
     7	# DOCX creation, editing, and analysis
     8	
     9	## Overview
    10	
    11	A .docx file is a ZIP archive containing XML files.
    12	
    13	## Quick Reference
    14	
    15	| Task | Approach |
    16	|------|----------|
    17	| Read/analyze content | `pandoc` or unpack for raw XML |
    18	| Create new document | Use `docx-js` - see Creating New Documents below |
    19	| Edit existing document | Unpack → edit XML → repack - see Editing Existing Documents below |
    20	
    21	### Converting .doc to .docx
    22	
    23	Legacy `.doc` files must be converted before editing:
    24	
    25	```bash
    26	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to docx document.doc
    27	```
    28	
    29	### Reading Content
    30	
    31	```bash
    32	# Text extraction with tracked changes
    33	pandoc --track-changes=all document.docx -o output.md
    34	
    35	# Raw XML access
    36	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
    37	```
    38	
    39	### Converting to Images
    40	
    41	```bash
    42	python scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf document.docx
    43	pdftoppm -jpeg -r 150 document.pdf page
    44	```
    45	
    46	### Accepting Tracked Changes
    47	
    48	To produce a clean document with all tracked changes accepted (requires LibreOffice):
    49	
    50	```bash
    51	python scripts/accept_changes.py input.docx output.docx
    52	```
    53	
    54	---
    55	
    56	## Creating New Documents
    57	
    58	Generate .docx files with JavaScript, then validate. Install: `npm install -g docx`
    59	
    60	### Setup
    61	```javascript
    62	const { Document, Packer, Paragraph, TextRun, Table, TableRow, TableCell, ImageRun,
    63	        Header, Footer, AlignmentType, PageOrientation, LevelFormat, ExternalHyperlink,
    64	        InternalHyperlink, Bookmark, FootnoteReferenceRun, PositionalTab,
    65	        PositionalTabAlignment, PositionalTabRelativeTo, PositionalTabLeader,
    66	        TabStopType, TabStopPosition, Column, SectionType,
    67	        TableOfContents, HeadingLevel, BorderStyle, WidthType, ShadingType,
    68	        VerticalAlign, PageNumber, PageBreak } = require('docx');
    69	
    70	const doc = new Document({ sections: [{ children: [/* content */] }] });
    71	Packer.toBuffer(doc).then(buffer => fs.writeFileSync("doc.docx", buffer));
    72	```
    73	
    74	### Validation
    75	After creating the file, validate it. If validation fails, unpack, fix the XML, and repack.
    76	```bash
    77	python scripts/office/validate.py doc.docx
    78	```
    79	
    80	### Page Size
    81	
    82	```javascript
    83	// CRITICAL: docx-js defaults to A4, not US Letter
    84	// Always set page size explicitly for consistent results
    85	sections: [{
    86	  properties: {
    87	    page: {
    88	      size: {
    89	        width: 12240,   // 8.5 inches in DXA
    90	        height: 15840   // 11 inches in DXA
    91	      },
    92	      margin: { top: 1440, right: 1440, bottom: 1440, left: 1440 } // 1 inch margins
    93	    }
    94	  },
    95	  children: [/* content */]
    96	}]
    97	```
    98	
    99	**Common page sizes (DXA units, 1440 DXA = 1 inch):**
   100	
   101	| Paper | Width | Height | Content Width (1" margins) |
   102	|-------|-------|--------|---------------------------|
   103	| US Letter | 12,240 | 15,840 | 9,360 |
   104	| A4 (default) | 11,906 | 16,838 | 9,026 |
   105	
   106	**Landscape orientation:** docx-js swaps width/height internally, so pass portrait dimensions and let it handle the swap:
   107	```javascript
   108	size: {
   109	  width: 12240,   // Pass SHORT edge as width
   110	  height: 15840,  // Pass LONG edge as height
   111	  orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE  // docx-js swaps them in the XML
   112	},
   113	// Content width = 15840 - left margin - right margin (uses the long edge)
   114	```
   115	
   116	### Styles (Override Built-in Headings)
   117	
   118	Use Arial as the default font (universally supported). Keep titles black for readability.
   119	
   120	```javascript
   121	const doc = new Document({
   122	  styles: {
   123	    default: { document: { run: { font: "Arial", size: 24 } } }, // 12pt default
   124	    paragraphStyles: [
   125	      // IMPORTANT: Use exact IDs to override built-in styles
   126	      { id: "Heading1", name: "Heading 1", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   127	        run: { size: 32, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   128	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 240, after: 240 }, outlineLevel: 0 } }, // outlineLevel required for TOC
   129	      { id: "Heading2", name: "Heading 2", basedOn: "Normal", next: "Normal", quickFormat: true,
   130	        run: { size: 28, bold: true, font: "Arial" },
   131	        paragraph: { spacing: { before: 180, after: 180 }, outlineLevel: 1 } },
   132	    ]
   133	  },
   134	  sections: [{
   135	    children: [
   136	      new Paragraph({ heading: HeadingLevel.HEADING_1, children: [new TextRun("Title")] }),
   137	    ]
   138	  }]
   139	});
   140	```
   141	
   142	### Lists (NEVER use unicode bullets)
   143	
   144	```javascript
   145	// ❌ WRONG - never manually insert bullet characters
   146	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("• Item")] })  // BAD
   147	new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("\u2022 Item")] })  // BAD
   148	
   149	// ✅ CORRECT - use numbering config with LevelFormat.BULLET
   150	const doc = new Document({
   151	  numbering: {
   152	    config: [
   153	      { reference: "bullets",
   154	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.BULLET, text: "•", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   155	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   156	      { reference: "numbers",
   157	        levels: [{ level: 0, format: LevelFormat.DECIMAL, text: "%1.", alignment: AlignmentType.LEFT,
   158	          style: { paragraph: { indent: { left: 720, hanging: 360 } } } }] },
   159	    ]
   160	  },
   161	  sections: [{
   162	    children: [
   163	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "bullets", level: 0 },
   164	        children: [new TextRun("Bullet item")] }),
   165	      new Paragraph({ numbering: { reference: "numbers", level: 0 },
   166	        children: [new TextRun("Numbered item")] }),
   167	    ]
   168	  }]
   169	});
   170	
   171	// ⚠️ Each reference creates INDEPENDENT numbering
   172	// Same reference = continues (1,2,3 then 4,5,6)
   173	// Different reference = restarts (1,2,3 then 1,2,3)
   174	```
   175	
   176	### Tables
   177	
   178	**CRITICAL: Tables need dual widths** - set both `columnWidths` on the table AND `width` on each cell. Without both, tables render incorrectly on some platforms.
   179	
   180	```javascript
   181	// CRITICAL: Always set table width for consistent rendering
   182	// CRITICAL: Use ShadingType.CLEAR (not SOLID) to prevent black backgrounds
   183	const border = { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 1, color: "CCCCCC" };
   184	const borders = { top: border, bottom: border, left: border, right: border };
   185	
   186	new Table({
   187	  width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Always use DXA (percentages break in Google Docs)
   188	  columnWidths: [4680, 4680], // Must sum to table width (DXA: 1440 = 1 inch)
   189	  rows: [
   190	    new TableRow({
   191	      children: [
   192	        new TableCell({
   193	          borders,
   194	          width: { size: 4680, type: WidthType.DXA }, // Also set on each cell
   195	          shading: { fill: "D5E8F0", type: ShadingType.CLEAR }, // CLEAR not SOLID
   196	          margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }, // Cell padding (internal, not added to width)
   197	          children: [new Paragraph({ children: [new TextRun("Cell")] })]
   198	        })
   199	      ]
   200	    })
   201	  ]
   202	})
   203	```
   204	
   205	**Table width calculation:**
   206	
   207	Always use `WidthType.DXA` — `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` breaks in Google Docs.
   208	
   209	```javascript
   210	// Table width = sum of columnWidths = content width
   211	// US Letter with 1" margins: 12240 - 2880 = 9360 DXA
   212	width: { size: 9360, type: WidthType.DXA },
   213	columnWidths: [7000, 2360]  // Must sum to table width
   214	```
   215	
   216	**Width rules:**
	< truncated lines 217-374 >
   375	}]
   376	```
   377	
   378	### Critical Rules for docx-js
   379	
   380	- **Set page size explicitly** - docx-js defaults to A4; use US Letter (12240 x 15840 DXA) for US documents
   381	- **Landscape: pass portrait dimensions** - docx-js swaps width/height internally; pass short edge as `width`, long edge as `height`, and set `orientation: PageOrientation.LANDSCAPE`
   382	- **Never use `\n`** - use separate Paragraph elements
   383	- **Never use unicode bullets** - use `LevelFormat.BULLET` with numbering config
   384	- **PageBreak must be in Paragraph** - standalone creates invalid XML
   385	- **ImageRun requires `type`** - always specify png/jpg/etc
   386	- **Always set table `width` with DXA** - never use `WidthType.PERCENTAGE` (breaks in Google Docs)
   387	- **Tables need dual widths** - `columnWidths` array AND cell `width`, both must match
   388	- **Table width = sum of columnWidths** - for DXA, ensure they add up exactly
   389	- **Always add cell margins** - use `margins: { top: 80, bottom: 80, left: 120, right: 120 }` for readable padding
   390	- **Use `ShadingType.CLEAR`** - never SOLID for table shading
   391	- **Never use tables as dividers/rules** - cells have minimum height and render as empty boxes (including in headers/footers); use `border: { bottom: { style: BorderStyle.SINGLE, size: 6, color: "2E75B6", space: 1 } }` on a Paragraph instead. For two-column footers, use tab stops (see Tab Stops section), not tables
   392	- **TOC requires HeadingLevel only** - no custom styles on heading paragraphs
   393	- **Override built-in styles** - use exact IDs: "Heading1", "Heading2", etc.
   394	- **Include `outlineLevel`** - required for TOC (0 for H1, 1 for H2, etc.)
   395	
   396	---
   397	
   398	## Editing Existing Documents
   399	
   400	**Follow all 3 steps in order.**
   401	
   402	### Step 1: Unpack
   403	```bash
   404	python scripts/office/unpack.py document.docx unpacked/
   405	```
   406	Extracts XML, pretty-prints, merges adjacent runs, and converts smart quotes to XML entities (`“` etc.) so they survive editing. Use `--merge-runs false` to skip run merging.
   407	
   408	### Step 2: Edit XML
   409	
   410	Edit files in `unpacked/word/`. See XML Reference below for patterns.
   411	
   412	**Use "Claude" as the author** for tracked changes and comments, unless the user explicitly requests use of a different name.
   413	
   414	**Use the Edit tool directly for string replacement. Do not write Python scripts.** Scripts introduce unnecessary complexity. The Edit tool shows exactly what is being replaced.
   415	
   416	**CRITICAL: Use smart quotes for new content.** When adding text with apostrophes or quotes, use XML entities to produce smart quotes:
   417	```xml
   418	<!-- Use these entities for professional typography -->
   419	<w:t>Here’s a quote: “Hello”</w:t>
   420	```
   421	| Entity | Character |
   422	|--------|-----------|
   423	| `‘` | ‘ (left single) |
   424	| `’` | ’ (right single / apostrophe) |
   425	| `“` | “ (left double) |
   426	| `”` | ” (right double) |
   427	
   428	**Adding comments:** Use `comment.py` to handle boilerplate across multiple XML files (text must be pre-escaped XML):
   429	```bash
   430	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Comment text with & and ’"
   431	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 1 "Reply text" --parent 0  # reply to comment 0
   432	python scripts/comment.py unpacked/ 0 "Text" --author "Custom Author"  # custom author name
   433	```
   434	Then add markers to document.xml (see Comments in XML Reference).
   435	
   436	### Step 3: Pack
   437	```bash
   438	python scripts/office/pack.py unpacked/ output.docx --original document.docx
   439	```
   440	Validates with auto-repair, condenses XML, and creates DOCX. Use `--validate false` to skip.
   441	
   442	**Auto-repair will fix:**
   443	- `durableId` >= 0x7FFFFFFF (regenerates valid ID)
   444	- Missing `xml:space="preserve"` on `<w:t>` with whitespace
   445	
   446	**Auto-repair won't fix:**
   447	- Malformed XML, invalid element nesting, missing relationships, schema violations
   448	
   449	### Common Pitfalls
   450	
   451	- **Replace entire `<w:r>` elements**: When adding tracked changes, replace the whole `<w:r>...</w:r>` block with `<w:del>...<w:ins>...` as siblings. Don't inject tracked change tags inside a run.
   452	- **Preserve `<w:rPr>` formatting**: Copy the original run's `<w:rPr>` block into your tracked change runs to maintain bold, font size, etc.
   453	
   454	---
   455	
   456	## XML Reference
   457	
   458	### Schema Compliance
   459	
   460	- **Element order in `<w:pPr>`**: `<w:pStyle>`, `<w:numPr>`, `<w:spacing>`, `<w:ind>`, `<w:jc>`, `<w:rPr>` last
   461	- **Whitespace**: Add `xml:space="preserve"` to `<w:t>` with leading/trailing spaces
   462	- **RSIDs**: Must be 8-digit hex (e.g., `00AB1234`)
   463	
   464	### Tracked Changes
   465	
   466	**Insertion:**
   467	```xml
   468	<w:ins w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   469	  <w:r><w:t>inserted text</w:t></w:r>
   470	</w:ins>
   471	```
   472	
   473	**Deletion:**
   474	```xml
   475	<w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   476	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   477	</w:del>
   478	```
   479	
   480	**Inside `<w:del>`**: Use `<w:delText>` instead of `<w:t>`, and `<w:delInstrText>` instead of `<w:instrText>`.
   481	
   482	**Minimal edits** - only mark what changes:
   483	```xml
   484	<!-- Change "30 days" to "60 days" -->
   485	<w:r><w:t>The term is </w:t></w:r>
   486	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   487	  <w:r><w:delText>30</w:delText></w:r>
   488	</w:del>
   489	<w:ins w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="...">
   490	  <w:r><w:t>60</w:t></w:r>
   491	</w:ins>
   492	<w:r><w:t> days.</w:t></w:r>
   493	```
   494	
   495	**Deleting entire paragraphs/list items** - when removing ALL content from a paragraph, also mark the paragraph mark as deleted so it merges with the next paragraph. Add `<w:del/>` inside `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`:
   496	```xml
   497	<w:p>
   498	  <w:pPr>
   499	    <w:numPr>...</w:numPr>  <!-- list numbering if present -->
   500	    <w:rPr>
   501	      <w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z"/>
   502	    </w:rPr>
   503	  </w:pPr>
   504	  <w:del w:id="2" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   505	    <w:r><w:delText>Entire paragraph content being deleted...</w:delText></w:r>
   506	  </w:del>
   507	</w:p>
   508	```
   509	Without the `<w:del/>` in `<w:pPr><w:rPr>`, accepting changes leaves an empty paragraph/list item.
   510	
   511	**Rejecting another author's insertion** - nest deletion inside their insertion:
   512	```xml
   513	<w:ins w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   514	  <w:del w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   515	    <w:r><w:delText>their inserted text</w:delText></w:r>
   516	  </w:del>
   517	</w:ins>
   518	```
   519	
   520	**Restoring another author's deletion** - add insertion after (don't modify their deletion):
   521	```xml
   522	<w:del w:author="Jane" w:id="5">
   523	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted text</w:delText></w:r>
   524	</w:del>
   525	<w:ins w:author="Claude" w:id="10">
   526	  <w:r><w:t>deleted text</w:t></w:r>
   527	</w:ins>
   528	```
   529	
   530	### Comments
   531	
   532	After running `comment.py` (see Step 2), add markers to document.xml. For replies, use `--parent` flag and nest markers inside the parent's.
   533	
   534	**CRITICAL: `<w:commentRangeStart>` and `<w:commentRangeEnd>` are siblings of `<w:r>`, never inside `<w:r>`.**
   535	
   536	```xml
   537	<!-- Comment markers are direct children of w:p, never inside w:r -->
   538	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   539	<w:del w:id="1" w:author="Claude" w:date="2025-01-01T00:00:00Z">
   540	  <w:r><w:delText>deleted</w:delText></w:r>
   541	</w:del>
   542	<w:r><w:t> more text</w:t></w:r>
   543	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   544	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   545	
   546	<!-- Comment 0 with reply 1 nested inside -->
   547	<w:commentRangeStart w:id="0"/>
   548	  <w:commentRangeStart w:id="1"/>
   549	  <w:r><w:t>text</w:t></w:r>
   550	  <w:commentRangeEnd w:id="1"/>
   551	<w:commentRangeEnd w:id="0"/>
   552	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="0"/></w:r>
   553	<w:r><w:rPr><w:rStyle w:val="CommentReference"/></w:rPr><w:commentReference w:id="1"/></w:r>
   554	```
   555	
   556	### Images
   557	
   558	1. Add image file to `word/media/`
   559	2. Add relationship to `word/_rels/document.xml.rels`:
   560	```xml
   561	<Relationship Id="rId5" Type=".../image" Target="media/image1.png"/>
   562	```
   563	3. Add content type to `[Content_Types].xml`:
   564	```xml
   565	<Default Extension="png" ContentType="image/png"/>
   566	```
   567	4. Reference in document.xml:
   568	```xml
   569	<w:drawing>
   570	  <wp:inline>
   571	    <wp:extent cx="914400" cy="914400"/>  <!-- EMUs: 914400 = 1 inch -->
   572	    <a:graphic>
   573	      <a:graphicData uri=".../picture">
   574	        <pic:pic>
   575	          <pic:blipFill><a:blip r:embed="rId5"/></pic:blipFill>
   576	        </pic:pic>
   577	      </a:graphicData>
   578	    </a:graphic>
   579	  </wp:inline>
   580	</w:drawing>
   581	```
   582	
   583	---
   584	
   585	## Dependencies
   586	
   587	- **pandoc**: Text extraction
   588	- **docx**: `npm install -g docx` (new documents)
   589	- **LibreOffice**: PDF conversion (auto-configured for sandboxed environments via `scripts/office/soffice.py`)
   590	- **Poppler**: `pdftoppm` for images
   591

content.text:
Here's your Know Your Numbers playbook. Each KPI block has the formula, a plain-English explanation, and a fill-in column so clients can plug in their own numbers on the spot. LTV is given its own featured section at the top with a step-by-step input table, a worked example, and a side-by-side "my LTV" box to complete.

Two things worth flagging:

**Weakest parts:**

1. The "Avg. Years as Client" row in the LTV table tells clients to "start with 2 years if unsure." That default is fine as a placeholder, but it can produce an artificially inflated LTV that gives false confidence. Consider adding a note that this number should be validated against actual client retention data within 30 days of onboarding.

2. The Contribution Margin block (KPI 06) is the most conceptually abstract of the 10 for an owner who doesn't have a finance background. A better version would include a two-line worked example directly in the explanation, not just in the formula box, showing the math failing on a discount promo so the lesson lands viscerally.
